catalog_quote: 2.4 STRESS. Like English, Broken has three degrees of stress: strong (primary), medium (secondary) and weak (tertiary). Most words borrowed from English follow the typical English word stress pattern and are pronounced with strong stress on their first syllable, secondary stress on their third and weak stress elsewhere. Words borrowed from the two traditional languages of the Strait tend to keep their original stress. There are exceptions to these rules and the stress pattern of individual words may differ according to the age of speakers and where they live. However, since stress is largely predictable, it is not marked here. [sec. 2.3, p. 12] The words of Broken, including compound words, can have one, two, three or four syllables, no matter what language they come from. ... Words of more than four syllables are reduced when borrowed into Broken, so that, for example, 'refrigerator' (five syllables) becomes prizareta (four syllables).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is etymologically stratified: the (majority) English-derived vocabulary mostly carries primary stress on the first syllable (secondary on the third), i.e. it follows English word stress; loans from Meriam Mir and Kala Lagaw Ya keep their source-language stress. The author treats stress as largely predictable and leaves it unmarked in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees of stress (primary, secondary, tertiary/weak); in English-derived words secondary stress typically falls on the third syllable. (Mittag 2016: 86 for Lockhart River Creole: English primary and secondary stresses are both retained, e.g. [ˌjuːniˈvɛːsiti].)
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are exceptions to these rules and the stress pattern of individual words may differ according to the age of speakers and where they live'; substrate-derived words (Meriam Mir in the eastern dialect, Kala Lagaw Ya in the western) keep original stress. Mittag (2016: 86) adds that Torres Strait Creole stress variation is 'lexically-, regionally-, and age-based'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress of lexical items (citation forms); compounds are said to have 'the same stress pattern as single words' (p. 21, ch. 6.3); object and subject pronouns 'usually unstressed'. Description is of the eastern-dialect sound system as the 'common core'.
new_statements.identity_note: Shnukal 1988 describes Torres Strait Creole ('Broken'), primarily the eastern dialect sound system (p. 13: 'The sound system described above is that of the eastern dialect of Broken'), with notes on the western dialect; this is the Torres Strait component of Glottolog's torr1261 'Torres Strait-Lockhart River Creole' (ISO tcs). Mittag 2016 describes Lockhart River Creole (Cape York Peninsula), the other named variety subsumed under torr1261; its stress statement (pp. 85-86) agrees in substance (English-derived words keep English stress; substrate-derived words keep source-language stress).

sources.note: Sec. 2.4 'Stress', p. 13: three degrees of stress as in English; most English-derived words have strong stress on the first syllable, secondary on the third, weak elsewhere; words from Meriam Mir / Kala Lagaw Ya keep their original stress; exceptions vary by age and region; stress largely predictable so not marked. Also p. 21/ch. 6: compounds have the stress pattern of single words; object pronouns usually unstressed; western-dialect transitive suffix -e > -i conditioned by the verb's stressed vowel.

sources.citation: Mittag, Joanna Ewa. 2016 [degree conferred 2017]. A Linguistic Description of Lockhart River Creole. PhD thesis, University of New England (Armidale). 462 pp. hdl:1959.11/22591
sources.note: Sec. 3.5.1 'Stress', pp. 85-86: 'Stress is lexically determined in LRC and depends on the stress of the original language'; English-derived vocabulary follows English stress placement, keeping both primary and secondary stress (e.g. [ˈlɛta], [ˌɛdjuˈkɛɪʃin]); the c. 1,300 Kuuku Ya'u/Umpila loans retain source stress (per Thompson 1988: primary on first vowel, or on the last long vowel if long vowels present); notes considerable lexically/regionally/age-based stress variation in Torres Strait Creole contra Shnukal's 'largely predictable'; compounds stressed on the initial syllable (ch. 4).

tone.quote: The intonational differences, which correlate highly with substrate language group and may in fact be due to the influence of these languages, are most usefully described here in musical terms. [...] Statements, questions and commands, the majority of which have falling intonation, may begin at a higher pitch for Easterners than for the others or end at a lower pitch. Sentence-internally, there are differences in pitch contour between the two groups. The eastern Islanders, whose speech is characterised by a marked rising and falling tone, use a greater pitch variation than do other speakers.
